summary: DINO PAD is a two-part health-monitoring system for astronauts on long missions to the Moon and Mars. The DINO PAD is a handheld prototype (ESP32, 2.8" color display, three buttons) that connects over Bluetooth LE to a Seeed SenseCAP T1000-E LoRa tracker running Meshtastic, shows the crew member's status on five tabs, and needs no Wi-Fi or internet to work. The Mission Base is a web app for the crew and flight surgeons: seven health indicators (heart rate, SpO2, body temperature, blood pressure, glucose, sleep, mood) with traffic-light status, an interactive human body, trends, alerts, an emergency protocol, a Mars sol clock and an estimated Earth–Mars signal delay. Each indicator explains why it matters and links to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight. Every value is labeled REAL, DEMO, NASA REFERENCE or USER LOG, so simulated data is never presented as measured. Today heart rate and SpO2 are simulated (our MAX30102 sensor has not arrived); battery, ambient temperature and light come from the real tracker.
details:
WHAT IT IS

DINO PAD is a health-monitoring system for astronauts on long missions (Moon, Mars), where crews must assess and act on their own health far from Earth. It has a device for the astronaut and a web app for the mission base.

HOW IT WORKS

1) DINO PAD (device): an ESP32 with a 2.8" color display, three buttons and 18650 batteries. A button-driven menu has five tabs (STATUS, ENVIRONMENT, TRACK, VITALS, MESSAGES). It connects over Bluetooth LE to a Seeed SenseCAP T1000-E tracker running Meshtastic (LoRa mesh) and reads real data from it: battery and voltage, channel use, uptime, ambient temperature and light (when enabled), and position when the GPS has a fix. The device does not need Wi-Fi or internet.

2) Mission Base (web app, PWA): seven indicators (heart rate, SpO2, body temperature, blood pressure, glucose, sleep, mood) with traffic-light status and normal ranges; an interactive human body (anatomy, 3D and 2D); trends, history and alerts; an emergency/SOS protocol; a Mars sol clock and an estimated Earth–Mars signal delay; an environment selector (ship, station, rover, Moon or Mars base, with gravity); a "Why it matters" explanation per indicator tied to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight (radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, closed and hostile environments); and a presentation mode.

HONESTY ABOUT DATA

Every value carries a label: REAL (measured by our hardware), DEMO (simulated by us), NASA REFERENCE (taken from a NASA/CSA source) or USER LOG (typed by the user, stored only in the browser). Today heart rate and SpO2 are DEMO because our MAX30102 sensor has not arrived. The positions on the Mars map are DEMO coordinates around Jezero Crater. The "normal ranges" are our project's values, not NASA's. The web app and the device are not yet linked end to end: the web uses a built-in simulator unless a backend is connected. Sending messages over LoRa is implemented but disabled in our demo build until we move to a private channel. This is not a medical device.

WHY IT IS DIFFERENT

We built the data source, not just the dashboard: a real device that talks to a real LoRa tracker, with an interface designed for the astronaut first and the base second. Nothing simulated is presented as real, and every health indicator explains itself in plain language, since astronauts should not need to be medical experts.

TOOLS

Hardware: ESP32, 2.8" ILI9341 TFT, Seeed SenseCAP T1000-E, 18650 cells and a power-bank module. Firmware: C++ with arduino-cli, NimBLE-Arduino, Adafruit GFX/ILI9341, nanopb with the Meshtastic protobufs. Web: React, Vite, three.js, a service worker (PWA), a FastAPI + MQTT backend, hosted on Cloudflare Pages.

NEXT STEPS

Add the MAX30102 (heart rate and SpO2), join device and web through the tracker, use a private LoRa channel, and validate ranges with NASA data.

USE OF AI

Code (device firmware and web), documentation and planning were developed with AI assistance (Anthropic's Claude: Claude Code and Claude chat). The team designed the system, wired and tested the hardware, and reviewed the results.
